The lighthouse stands at the edge of the world, or at least the edge of someone’s world. Its white wall is salt-stained, its iron stairway cold even in summer, and its lamp turns through the dark with a patience that feels almost holy. Ships no longer need it as they once did, yet it remains useful in another way: as a reminder that guidance can be quiet, steady, and distant without being indifferent.

I like to think of the keeper who once climbed those stairs each evening, carrying oil, trimming wicks, polishing glass. His work was repetitive, but repetition is not always emptiness. Sometimes it is devotion. Every night he made a small circle of light against a huge night, and somewhere out on the water that circle meant safety, direction, a chance to come home.

We all need lighthouses, though not all of them are towers on cliffs. A phrase from a friend can be one. A book opened at the right moment can be one. A memory of kindness that returns when we are lost can be one. They do not solve every problem or calm every storm. They simply mark something fixed, something reliable, enough to steer by.

Perhaps that is why the image endures. The sea changes, the weather turns, and the shore itself is slowly rewritten by waves. But the lighthouse remains, saying without words: here is the rock, here is the warning, here is the way back. And sometimes that is enough for us.
